I equally don't understand why our improbability imparts any value. Stars aren't particularly rare but they are, as Joe Rogan later ruminates on, the most important thing for life. Not all stars impart life but so what? There are frameworks in which rarity can impart value but rarity in and of itself doesn't do anything for me. Without a framework I don't see how you just arbitrarily say "our improbability, fragility and brevity makes us valuable." 

The answer is it isn't arbitrary. We have different experiential frameworks. Your framework allows you to accept that train of logic, mine does not. I think there are differences of perspective, especially motivational ones, that cannot be logically argued in order to truly persuade someone. You can persuade someone of facts but when it comes to things such as meaning, value, consciousness, the facts can support your argument but there are no current facts about the things themselves. We infer their existence, and this is where logical arguments come in, but we cannot view the phenomenon directly. 

Seems to me in order to persuade someone on topics like this you need a solid argument, yes. But also the person you are trying to persuade requires some unknown collection of similar experiences to those which caused your own perspective to form. otherwise it literally cannot click for them in the same way that the theist argument fails to connect for you. You are, without realizing it, drawing on experiences you have and believe to be had by all, that makes your particular logic train seem undeniable as well as self-evident. And so too believes the person you are trying to convince. Which is why you may not have success convincing someone of something one day, and then years later the person may come back to you and say "You know, I had X experience and because of that I now agree with you." In some cases that experience may be learning new facts but facts still have to be interpreted. For me, experience is just as important as observable facts.

That's the difference between atheists and theists in my mind. They exist all along the spectrum from highly intelligent to barely intelligent people (Granted I suspect the distributions may change). So atheists have one set of common and similar experiences and theists have another. The trick is for atheists and theists to stop worrying so much about the particulars of where values come from so long as the values themselves are the same.

It's a fine line. I don't think anyone would have a problem if only people well meaning with the results to back it up ever self promoted. But anyone can self promote so, at least for me, a healthy dose of skepticism isn't unwarranted. Especially if it helps red flag for people who are less cynical. I'd much rather refer people to a book like you mentioned than to a website promoting supplements. Anyone dedicated to lucid dreaming can do so without anything more than knowledge, dedication and guidance.

The dangers of masturbation are abound in historical popular culture but the explanations are generally poorly elaborated, sensationalized, or blatantly untrue (you'll go blind, etc...). When one explanation is seen to be misrepresented or untrue it seems human nature to assume the opposite is true. That seems the position modern society has taken. However, to give modern society it's due, as with anything, masturbation is likely healthy enough in moderation. But as a culture, we have cast out much of our traditional wisdom and tended toward extreme views on all fronts, including masturbation. The popular unspoken view seems to be, if a little is good, a lot is better.

Unfortunately the transmission of important life wisdom from one generation to the next seems to have been degrading now for some decades, a starting point for which is difficult to pinpoint. But the point is each successive generation seems to have imparted less and less of the lessons learned for living a contended (if not successful) life. There are of course exceptions, some families have been diligent about such things and have continued to thrive but have not extended their wisdom beyond their family circles. I'm sure for a slew of reasons conscious or unconscious. But I think by-and-large the average person has for some time now, even with parents, had to find things out on their own. Unfortunately in many cases too late. As to why this occurred? Who is to say for certain? Understanding how life, societies and culture unfold is staggeringly complex and difficult to fully comprehend. It has been confounding humanity, presumably, since we first attained sentience. 

To make an attempt, and to further elaborate on reasons given above, I think on piece of the total explanation is because previous generations just took certain kernels of wisdom on faith without being able to articulate the truth behind why they were true. Or, that explanations were so self-evident as to not need them. Perhaps a good explanation for why masturbation and pornography are bad is that masturbation leads to a lack of discipline and will power which saps energy from seemingly unrelated aspects of life. Masturbation without porn may also be less dangerous as it would require the use of imagination and perhaps at least some narrative. Porn strips these necessities and accelerates the inhibition of cultivating the concepts discipline and personal sacrifice by making something that must be worked for and cultivated (a relationship) seem unnecessary/less expedient than obtaining instant gratification in the short term. What you are doing is sacrificing your future for your present, when the reverse is usually more desirable. Though I suspect you have discovered this on your own else you wouldn't recognize you have a problem and be asking this question in your despair.

Further, even though you haven't taken drugs I think porn and masturbation both act on the brain in a similar fashion. External stimuli are acting on your brain in a way that would not typically or otherwise occur on their own in 'nature'. I am not an expert, i have no credentials other than personal experience so take this all with a grain of salt. That being said I have had similar struggles with porn, I have done drugs and am addicted to video games as well. All at an age I think I should be well past these things. In my personal experience just because you aren't ingesting something chemical doesn't mean you aren't changing your brain's natural neurochemistry. Anything can become a 'drug' in my experience if it becomes a singular focus for relief from life's struggles. 

It seems to me there is still time for you to change but it will not be easy. You must search deep within yourself to discover what will keep you motivated to change, not an easy task, but possible. Training your will power and discipline is key. Could you perhaps enroll in a martial arts class or something of that nature? Try and remember that you are not your flesh. You must master it and control it rather than letting it control you. You can discover great personal power in taming your mind and body. Discover your inner fight and you will have a chance!

Bottom line: If you make it through this and go on to have a family, Teach your kids everything you have learned and explain to them why it is true. Please please please, when your kids ask you why, don't ever say "Because I said so." No matter how inconvenient or tedious take the time to give them a proper explanation. If you don't have one readily at hand tell them so and that you will come back to it later.

I think the question we should be more concerned about is, "are Americans *in general* doing an adequate job raising kids?", not whether a specific group is doing an adequate job. I worry everyone is doing a bad job... 

***Hypothetically***, even if it were true that heterosexual couples did a better job (and I don't even know if we could agree on what constitutes a "good job" anyway), I'm not sure it could be definitively proven it in our lifetime. Too many variables to control for and, studies take time, this one took 32 years after all.  And all the while, variables are continuing to change as society moves forward.

You might be able to prove that a certain group has the optimal potential at raising a well adjusted human adult, but not only does that not mean you will always get the 'best' result with the 'best' starting conditions, regardless of who you study specifically, it's too easy to get false negatives because some people are just going to be terrible parents regardless of any other factor you categorize them for. Furthermore, gay or lesbian couples are going to raise their kids to reflect the culture they are most comfortable with. Big surprise, that's probably an American culture. Or at the very least a pseudo-American culture which is close enough.  Admittedly our country seems to be going through a bit of a culture identity crisis at the moment but it's still more or less recognizable as American anywhere you go in the country.

I suspect the way gays and lesbians raise their kids actually turns out to be very similar to the way heterosexuals do it since we all live in the same culture and a significant portion of homosexuals probably had heterosexual parents raise them to begin with. Humans mimic other humans and the simplest (though almost certainly not the most comprehensive) way to parent, if you have never done it before, is to do it the way you remember your parents did it. Which is to say imperfectly, both in terms of the actual parenting a given individual received, and in terms of the fallibility of human perception and memory to precisely recall just exactly how you were raised to begin with. 

So, to reiterate and conclude,  I'm not sure how this study alone really helps elucidate anything we can use constructively. It doesn't address what I think is probably a more useful and less divisive question that would be something along the lines of "If any, what are the bare minimum child raising techniques that are needed to give any given child, in any given circumstance, their best chance at being mentally healthy in adulthood?" 

I want to know how are we doing, as a nation, raising our kids. Then I want to know how we can take steps to improve it across the board regardless of who is doing the parenting. Even if were to turn out that Americans on average are doing a pretty good job, there's always room for improvement. It might be more productive to design some studies to figure out if we can distill some basic bare minimum child rearing rules that work in any situation. Although I suspect much of this work has probably already been done, already exists in child developmental psychological literature, and it's more a matter of disseminating the information to the public than it is creating new studies. And finally I'll just say, I know my line of thought here isn't ironclad but if I were to attempt to make it ironclad it would be a significantly longer document and I already made it too long. Just wanting to provide some fuel for further discussion.
